summary: Documents the list of numbers assigned for networks, protocols and similar identifiers, and replaces a number of earlier lists. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 900.

eli5.summary: A big phone book of network numbers that replaced older copies.

questions: class a b c ip networks
subtitle: The early registry of assigned network numbers, protocol identifiers, and port numbers

tldr.problem: As the early internet grew, many systems needed to assign and track network numbers (for identifying subnets), IP version numbers, protocol numbers (for identifying the next layer), and port numbers (for identifying services).
tldr.mechanism: This RFC documents all assigned numbers as of October 1983, organized by category. It establishes three classes of IP addresses (A, B, C) and lists what networks are assigned in each class, as well as all protocol and port assignments, providing a stable reference.
tldr.outcome: This becomes the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) registry, the authoritative source for these assignments. RFC 870 is Historic, replaced by RFC 900 and later automated registries. It represents the moment before explosive growth made manual registries obsolete.

today: RFC 870 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 900 (June 1984) and is now superseded by the IANA online registry. Modern address space is managed under Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), which does not use the Class A/B/C scheme defined here.

sections.title: Purpose and Organization
sections.content:
RFC 870 documents the currently assigned values for network numbers, Internet version numbers, protocol numbers, and port numbers used in ARPANET and early Internet implementations. It consolidates what had previously been scattered across many RFCs and IENs (Internet Experiment Notes). Joyce Reynolds, the RFC's co-author with Jon Postel, managed number assignments and updated this document periodically as new allocations were made.

The RFC establishes that anyone developing a new protocol or application requiring a network number, protocol number, port number, or other identifier must contact the central assignment authority to receive an officially recognized number. This centralized approach ensures no collisions and provides a single authoritative reference.
sections.eli5: This document is the official rule book for how computers get their internet numbers and codes. Everything that needs a unique number comes through here.

sections.title: IP Address Classes and Network Numbers
sections.content:
The RFC defines the IP address structure as three classes to accommodate networks of different sizes. Class A networks have a 7-bit network number (allowing 128 networks) and 24-bit local addresses, for organizations needing hundreds of thousands of hosts. Class B networks have a 14-bit network number (allowing 16,384 networks) and 16-bit local addresses, for medium-sized organizations. Class C networks have a 21-bit network number (allowing over 2 million networks) and 8-bit local addresses (256 hosts each), for small organizations.

The RFC lists which networks have been assigned in each class, using dotted-decimal notation (four 8-bit fields separated by periods). As of October 1983, 1,117 networks had been assigned for active Internet use (14 Class A, 37 Class B, 1,066 Class C), with additional allocations made for future expansion. Network numbers are categorized as Research (R), Defense (D), or Commercial (C).
sections.eli5: Computers on the internet need numbers. Big networks get short numbers, small networks get longer ones. This book lists which numbers have been used and who owns them.

sections.title: Protocol and Version Numbers
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) header contains a 4-bit version field and an 8-bit protocol field. The version field identifies the format of the IP header itself; as of 1983, version 4 is the standard (later replaced by IPv6). The protocol field identifies which upper-layer protocol follows the IP header: ICMP (control messages), TCP (reliable streams), UDP (datagrams), EGP (exterior gateway routing), or various experimental protocols.

The RFC lists all assigned version numbers (0-15) and protocol numbers (0-255), noting which are reserved, unassigned, or in use. TCP is protocol 6, UDP is protocol 17 (21 octal). Protocols used by various research networks (XEROX NS, MIT Subnet Support, SATNET Monitoring) also appear in the list, showing the diversity of experimental protocols that coexisted on the early Internet.
sections.eli5: Data traveling across the network carries tags that say what kind of information it is and which format it uses. These tags have assigned numbers so computers know what to expect.

sections.title: Port Numbers for Services
sections.content:
TCP and UDP both use port numbers to identify which application process receives data arriving at a host. The RFC reserves a small range of "well-known" port numbers for standard services. Telnet uses port 23, SMTP (mail) uses port 25, Domain Name System (DNS) uses port 53, and so on. These assignments allow servers to listen on known ports where clients expect to find them.

The RFC notes that the same port assignments are reused between TCP and UDP where possible. The list shows ports for file transfer (FTP), remote login (Telnet), electronic mail (SMTP and its related protocols), and specialized research services. Many port numbers remain unassigned, reserved for future use.
sections.eli5: When you connect to a computer, you need to know which door to knock on. Port numbers are those doors. Common services always use the same door numbers so programs know where to find them.

sections.title: Assignment Authority and Process
sections.content:
Assignments are coordinated by a central authority (Joyce Reynolds at USC-ISI in 1983) through either formal RFCs or direct application. The document lists the responsible individual for each assignment in the right margin, allowing network administrators to contact the owner if questions arise about a particular network or protocol.

The RFC distinguishes between numbers assigned for Internet use (interoperable across ARPA and DoD networks), numbers allocated for Internet use (assigned but not yet deployed), and the theoretical maximum allowed (far beyond what is needed, providing room for future growth). As of October 1983, only a tiny fraction of the available address and protocol space had been used.
sections.eli5: The assignment authority is like a librarian: they keep track of who gets which numbers and make sure no one gets the same number twice.

sections.title: Historical Significance and Transition
sections.content:
RFC 870 represents a snapshot of the early Internet at a moment of rapid growth. It consolidates assignments from earlier RFCs (503, 433, 349, 290, 776, 790, 820) and several IENs. The address space is arranged in three classes, which will later prove inadequate for the explosion of hosts in the 1990s, eventually giving way to Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR).

This is the last edition that could plausibly be printed on paper as a complete, readable document. Subsequent editions (RFC 900 and beyond) grew too large, and assignment of numbers eventually moved to online databases and automated registries maintained by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), ARIN (American Registry for Internet Numbers), and regional authorities.
sections.eli5: This book was the last time anyone could print the whole internet address book on paper. Soon the internet got too big and had to use computers to keep track of all the numbers.
